# File-type filtering in the `ignore` crate

ripgrep's `-t/--type`, `-T/--type-not`, `--type-add` and `--type-clear` flags
are backed entirely by one module: `crates/ignore/src/types.rs`, with the
shipped definitions living beside it in `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`.
Nothing about the CLI lives here. `types.rs` is a self-contained library that
turns a set of named glob definitions and a set of user selections into a
matcher. The `crates/core` glue that reads flags is thin, and we cover it last.

## How a type definition is represented

A single type is a `FileTypeDef`: a `name: String` and a `globs: Vec<String>`.
That's the whole model. The Rust type is `*.rs`; the C type is `*.[chH]`,
`*.[chH].in`, `*.cats`. A name can carry many globs, and (through the default
table) many names can share one glob list.

The defaults are a flat const table, not code:

```rust
pub(crate) const DEFAULT_TYPES: &[(&[&str], &[&str])] = &[
    (&["rust"], &["*.rs"]),
    (&["cpp"], &["*.[ChH]", "*.cc", "*.[ch]pp", /* ... */]),
    // ...
];
```

Each row is `(names, extensions)`. The first slice is a list of aliases (for
example `bat` and `batch` name the same globs), and `add_defaults` expands the
whole cross-product by calling `add(name, ext)` for every name against every
glob. So adding a format means adding one row here, keeping it wrapped to 79
columns and sorted. The sort isn't cosmetic: a `#[cfg(test)]` test,
`default_types_are_sorted`, asserts the first alias of each row is strictly
greater than the previous, so an out-of-order insert fails `cargo test`.

## Building a definition set: `TypesBuilder`

`TypesBuilder` holds a `HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>` of definitions plus a
`Vec<Selection<()>>` of what the user asked for. You populate definitions three
ways:

- `add(name, glob)` appends one glob to a named def, creating it if absent. The
  name must be non-empty and every character `is_alphanumeric()`, and the
  literal name `all` is reserved, so both return `Error::InvalidDefinition`.
- `add_def(def)` parses the string form used on the command line. Split on `:`,
  it accepts `{name}:{glob}` (a root definition) or
  `{name}:include:{comma,separated,names}` (an aggregate that copies the globs
  of already-defined types). `include` validates every referenced type up front
  and fails without mutating state if one is missing, so a bad `--type-add`
  leaves the builder untouched.
- `add_defaults()` loads `DEFAULT_TYPES` as above.

`select(name)` and `negate(name)` push a `Selection::Select` or
`Selection::Negate`. Both special-case `all` to fan out over every currently
defined name. `clear(name)` drops a definition entirely.

## Compiling to a matcher: `build`

`build()` produces the immutable `Types`. It walks the ordered selections, and
for each one looks up its `FileTypeDef` (an unknown name is
`Error::UnrecognizedFileType`). Every glob of every selected or negated def is
compiled through `globset::GlobBuilder::new(glob).literal_separator(true)` and
added to a `GlobSetBuilder`. `literal_separator(true)` matters: it stops `*`
from crossing `/`, so these globs match against a bare file name rather than a
path.

Two side tables fall out of this loop. `glob_to_selection: Vec<(usize, usize)>`
maps each glob's index in the compiled `GlobSet` back to the selection that
owns it and its position within that def. `has_selected` records whether any
selection was a `Select` (as opposed to only negations); it's the switch that
decides what an unmatched file becomes.

## Matching

`Types::matched(path, is_dir)` returns a `Match<Glob>`, the crate's three-valued
`None` / `Ignore` / `Whitelist`. Directories and an empty glob set short-circuit
to `Match::None`. Otherwise it extracts the base name with
`pathutil::file_name` and runs `GlobSet::matches_into`, which fills a
`Vec<usize>` of every matching glob index. The scratch `Vec` comes from an
`Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>` (`regex_automata`'s pool), because the directory walk
calls `matched` from many threads and this avoids per-call allocation.

Precedence is positional: the last index in the match list wins. ripgrep
resolves that glob back through `glob_to_selection` to its `Selection`. A
`Negate` yields `Match::Ignore`, a `Select` yields `Match::Whitelist`. If
nothing matched, `has_selected` decides: with at least one selection, a
non-match is `Match::Ignore` (you asked for a type and this isn't it); with only
negations, it's `Match::None`. Because precedence follows selection order, and
selection order follows command-line order, later flags override earlier ones.

## Where it plugs in

`crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs::types` is the only wiring: it calls
`add_defaults()`, replays each `TypeChange` (`Clear`, `Add`, `Select`,
`Negate`) onto a `TypesBuilder`, and builds. The resulting `Types` is handed to
`IgnoreBuilder::types` in `crates/ignore/src/dir.rs`, where it participates in
the walk's match stack alongside gitignore matching.

## What a contributor should know

Adding a format is a one-line, well-tested edit to `DEFAULT_TYPES`: keep it
sorted and under 79 columns. Changing the matcher itself means respecting three
invariants that the code depends on but doesn't loudly announce: globs are built
with `literal_separator(true)` and matched against the base name only;
`glob_to_selection` must stay index-aligned with the `GlobSet` you feed the
builder; and last-match-wins is the precedence contract users rely on. `Types`
is immutable and `Clone`, so all mutation belongs in `TypesBuilder`.
